title: Bhagyachandra Dreams the Ras Lila
subtitle: Exile, Vision, and the Birth of the Ras Lila
era: Bhagyachandra's reigns and artistic reforms, 1759-1798 CE
region: Imphal, Assam, Moirang and Vaishnava Manipur
moral: Art can rebuild identity after exile.

sources.citation: Parratt, The Court Chronicle of the Kings of Manipur, Vols. 1-2 (2005, 2009)
sources.note: Chronicle evidence for Bhagyachandra, exile, return and Ras Lila traditions.

sources.citation: Rodney Sebastian, Cultural Fusion in a Religious Dance Drama (University of Florida, 2019)
sources.note: Recent detailed study of Manipuri Ras Lila as religious and political performance.

sources.citation: Moirangthem Kirti Singh, Religious Developments in Manipur in the 18th and 19th Centuries (1980)
sources.note: Classic study of the Vaishnavite transformation and Bhagyachandra's religious world.

panels.shot: dramatic mid-shot in twilight, king half in shadow, temple silhouette behind

dialogue.text: In an age of exile and war, King Bhagya Chandra of Manipur dreamed a dance—and turned a wounded kingdom into a moving circle around Govindaji.

panels.shot: epic bird’s-eye of Imphal valley with fort and surrounding hills

dialogue.text: Mid-eighteenth century. Manipur is a hill-ringed valley between Burma and Assam, its kings balancing tribute, raids and trade along the eastern frontier of the subcontinent.

panels.shot: slow push-in on king’s face, brows furrowed, listening to a courtier’s unseen report

dialogue.text: The chronicles call him Ching-Thang Khomba, later remembered as Bhagya Chandra. His throne stands between Ahom Assam to the west and the expanding Burmese kingdom to the east.

panels.shot: wide shot of palace courtyard with soldiers scattering as flames rise in distance

dialogue.text: Conflict with Burma intensifies. Raids, counter-raids, shifting alliances. At one point, the Manipur court is broken and the king is driven from his own valley.

panels.shot: long shot of a small royal group on the move through forested hills

dialogue.text: The court chronicle records exile. The king leaves his homeland, seeking safety and allies in the west, toward the Ahom kingdom of Assam.

panels.shot: wide shot of Ahom court hall in Gargaon, with Bhagya Chandra standing before the throne

dialogue.text: In Assam, he turns from fugitive to guest. The Ahom court weighs his plea: help him regain Manipur, and a buffer against Burma will be restored.

panels.shot: medium close-up of Bhagya Chandra at night, seated cross-legged, eyes closed in devotion

dialogue.text: By this time, Vaishnava devotion, shaped by Gaudiya bhakti, has reached Manipur. In exile, Bhagya Chandra turns inward, deepening his worship of Krishna.

panels.shot: dreamlike wide shot of a moonlit field where Krishna and gopis dance in a circle

dialogue.text: Court tradition says that in this time he dreams Krishna. Not a simple vision, but a circle of dancers around the dark cowherd, the Ras, under a moon that feels like home.

panels.shot: close-up on Bhagya Chandra waking, sweat on his brow, eyes bright with resolve

dialogue.speaker: king_bhagya_chandra
dialogue.text: If I return, Govindaji will stand in Manipur, and the Ras will be his worship.

panels.shot: wide shot of Manipuri and Ahom forces marching together through a valley

dialogue.text: The chronicles note Ahom help. With Assamese support, the exiled king leads forces back through the passes, aiming to reclaim the Imphal valley from Burmese-backed rivals.

panels.shot: dynamic wide shot of battle lines facing each other on a plain, without gore

dialogue.text: There are clashes, losses, negotiations. The war is hard, but by the later 1760s, his position in Manipur is restored. Exile ends; rule resumes.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of the king entering Kangla fort, people bowing on either side

dialogue.text: But the valley he returns to is not the same. War has scattered families, shaken old rituals, and left a question: what now binds Manipur together?

panels.shot: wide shot of a sacred grove where traditional Lai Haraoba is being performed

dialogue.text: For centuries, Lai Haraoba had told the valley’s old stories—of deities, creation, and the land itself. Now Vaishnava bhakti presses in, asking for new forms of devotion.

panels.shot: medium shot of the king in council with Brahmanas, gurus, and traditional priests

dialogue.text: Historians like Moirangthem Kirti Singh describe a kingdom negotiating change. The king stands at the meeting point of Gaudiya Vaishnavism and older Meitei ritual life.

panels.shot: mid-shot of the king overseeing artisans carving an image of Krishna

dialogue.text: The chronicles credit him with installing Govindaji, a Krishna image, as Manipur’s royal deity. For the king, this is both devotion and statecraft—a divine center for a fragmented land.

panels.shot: wide shot of a temple courtyard with Govindaji idol raised on a pedestal

dialogue.speaker: king_bhagya_chandra
dialogue.text: From this day, our kingdom circles his feet, not my throne.

panels.shot: medium shot of the king with drummers and dance teachers, pointing to a scroll

dialogue.text: Around 1779, tradition says, he turns his dream into discipline. With drummers and gurus, he shapes a new Ras Lila, drawing from Lai Haraoba, Pung Cholom and martial movement.

panels.shot: gentle mid-shot of the king speaking to a young princess in ornate costume

dialogue.text: Sources agree: he places his daughter Bimbamati as Radha. Royal blood steps into the role of the soul, turning the Ras into both worship and royal statement.

panels.shot: wide, frontal shot of the first Ras Lila performance in a temple courtyard

dialogue.text: The Ras Lila rises: measured steps, curved hands, controlled spins. Old Meitei gestures now retell Vaishnava stories, turning the battlefield generation into a disciplined ring around Krishna.

panels.shot: close-up of the king’s eyes reflecting the circling dancers

dialogue.speaker: king_bhagya_chandra
dialogue.text: Let them remember this circle longer than they remember our wars.

panels.shot: wide shot of later generations performing Ras Lila, with a faded overlay of the king

dialogue.text: Modern scholars trace manuscripts, temple practice and performance lineages. Beyond legend, they see a deliberate royal project: art as policy, devotion as a way to rebuild identity after exile.

panels.shot: final contemplative wide shot of Manipur valley with a Ras Lila pavilion glowing at night

dialogue.text: Bhagya Chandra’s reign ends, but the Ras circle endures. In it, a small frontier kingdom still remembers how one exiled king turned loss into a living, moving theology around Govindaji.
